stem: A 38-year-old man presents with recurrent peptic ulcers that have not responded to proton pump inhibitor therapy. Fasting gastrin levels are found to be markedly elevated. He also reports occasional diarrhea and abdominal discomfort. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Stomach and Duodenum) Source note (Final 442 F Q3): The related recall of treatment-resistant ulcers with chronic watery diarrhea gives A. Neuroendocrine tumor. Answer: A.
expl: PPI-refractory recurrent ulcers + markedly raised fasting gastrin + diarrhoea = gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome).

why.B: Responds to eradication/PPI; gastrin not markedly high.
why.D: Not with high gastrin and diarrhoea.

stem: What is the most common site of gastrinoma (excluding the pancreas)?
expl: Most gastrinomas lie in the gastrinoma triangle; outside the pancreas, the duodenum (2nd/3rd part) is the commonest site — duodenal gastrinomas are now the most frequent overall.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a history of yellowish discoloration of sclera and skin with dark urine and pale stool for one month. On examination he was jaundiced with palpable distended gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
srcNote: (Hepato-bilio-pancreatic neoplasms) Source note (Final 427 F Q56 (p. 316)): Courvoisier’s sign (or law) describes an enlarged, palpable gallbladder in patients with obstructive jaundice caused by tumors of the biliary tree or by pancreatic head tumors.
expl: Painless progressive obstructive jaundice in an elderly man with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier) = malignant distal obstruction → carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

why.A: Gallbladder is usually fibrosed/not palpable; painful, fluctuating jaundice.
why.B: Hilar tumour — gallbladder collapsed, not palpable.
why.D: Stone in the gallbladder neck compressing the CHD — pain, gallbladder not distended.

stem: 70yo fell from bed, he is asymptomatic, CT showed pancreatic cyst in the side duct, main duct not affected. Cyst size: 2.5 cm. What's the most appropriate management?
expl: Asymptomatic side-branch IPMN 1–3 cm without worrisome features → imaging every 6 months for 2 years, then yearly.

stem: A case of an old patient who was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma was resected. Few years later he presented with a hypervascular lesion in the tail of the pancreas. It was highly suspended of RCC metastasis. What is the next step in management?
srcNote: (not sure) (Hepato-bilio-pancreatic neoplasms) Uncertain source key: the original answer is marked "not sure".
expl: Source key A (marked "not sure"). A hypervascular pancreatic tail lesion after RCC = RCC metastasis; isolated RCC metastases benefit from resection → distal pancreatectomy.

why.D: Not needed; tissue diagnosis isn't required before resection.

stem: Diaphoretic patient, hypoglycemic return to normal after juice intake. He has a mass in the tail of the pancreas on CTt how to confirm the Dx?
expl: Insulinoma is confirmed biochemically: hypoglycaemia with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide (endogenous insulin) — insulin/glucose ratio >0.3.

why.D: Imaging localises, doesn't confirm hormone excess.

stem: What is the tumor marker for pancreatic head tumor?
srcNote: ( Surgical oncology) The source prints option B as "CA19-1"; the original wording and key are preserved.
expl: CA 19-9 is the pancreatic (and biliary) tumor marker ("CA19-1" here is a typo for 19-9).

stem: A 67-year-old man went to his family physician complaining of a lump in the right groin. The patient's history is consistent with inguinal hernia, but the doctor could not appreciate it on examination so he ordered a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis. CT scan showed no inguinal hernia, but simple lipoma in the right groin. An incidental finding on the scan showed a pancreas cyst consistent with Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), with pancreatic main duct dilatation around 12 mm.
srcNote: The source provides the clinical scenario and management options without a separate question sentence.
expl: Main-duct IPMN with duct ≥10 mm is a high-risk stigma (malignancy 60–80%) → surgical resection (here distal pancreatectomy for a body/tail lesion).

stem: A case of an old patient with confirmed adenocarcinoma in the head of the pancreas, which one of the following is the treatment of choice?
expl: Resectable pancreatic head adenocarcinoma → pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple) + adjuvant chemotherapy.

stem: Which ONE of the following represents Courvoisier's law in a 75-year-old patient with obstructive jaundice?

opts.t: Gallbladder is palpable the jaundice is unlikely to be due to stone
Gallbladder is palpable the jaundice is due to common bile duct stone
Gallbladder is not palpable the jaundice is due to common hepatic stone
Gallbladder is not palpable the jaundice is due to pancreatic

srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders) Incomplete option D: the wording ends at "pancreatic" in the source.
expl: Courvoisier's law: in a jaundiced patient a palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be due to stones (chronic cholecystitis makes the gallbladder fibrotic and non-distensible) → suspect malignancy (pancreatic head/periampullary).
